hero.headline: Put the brain on a schedule
hero.sub: An automation is a headless Claude run on a cadence you set, with nobody at the keyboard. You describe the job in plain language; one dispatcher wakes every five minutes, runs what is due, writes a dated document, and tells you what it found.

shot.alt: The Automations page before you own one: the headline "Put the brain on a schedule" over a diagram of three scheduled jobs feeding one dispatcher, which spawns a headless claude session that writes an output file, sends a notification, and reads and updates a pattern
shot.caption: The whole loop, before you write your first one.

blocks.title: A job is a prompt and a clock
blocks.body: There is no built-in "digest" command and no hardcoded job type. The manifest's ## Prompt section is the whole job; the CLI carries only the schedule, the model, the reasoning effort and the timeout. If you can write it as a prompt, it can be an automation.

shot.alt: Three automation cards: End of day digest every day at 18:00 with a last run this afternoon, Dependency drift check on Tuesdays at 09:00, and Friday weekly report at 17:00, each with a Run now button

blocks.title: It learns from every run
blocks.body: A job that starts from zero every time repeats its mistakes forever, and nobody is watching it happen. So each automation keeps a pattern in its own manifest: a standing playbook plus a short ledger of lessons, read before every run and added to after one. A job that hit a broken endpoint on Sunday knows that next Sunday.

shot.alt: The pattern of a real automation: a playbook the run wrote itself describing the order to gather in, above four dated lessons about which commands work on this vault
shot.caption: Every line here was written by the run itself, through the CLI, never by hand.

blocks.title: You can read what a run actually did
blocks.body: The output document is the conclusion with the working thrown away, which is the wrong half the moment a run surprises you. The session drill-in replays the headless run turn by turn: every tool call and its argument, which ones failed, how many turns it took and what it cost.

shot.alt: A run's session: 32 tool calls, 2 failed, 33 turns, $1.8097, above the list of Bash calls it made, with two of them marked in red

blocks.title: Because it runs unattended, it is locked down by default

items.title: Nothing runs until you say so
items.text: The whole subsystem ships disabled. You install the dispatcher yourself, and approve each automation on this machine, before anything fires.

items.title: Approval is a hash of what will happen
items.text: The prompt, output instructions, model, effort, timeout, output directory and whether it learns are hashed. Change any of them — including a teammate's synced edit — and the job stops until a human reviews it again.

items.title: Private to this machine
items.text: A new automation, its run history and its output stay off your team's shared brain until you run automations share. Unsharing stops future publishing; it does not retrieve what already left.

items.title: The notification says what happened
items.text: Not "a file was written" — the run's own result sentence, titled by the automation, with the document as a click target. Success and failure sound different.

blocks.text: The pattern is deliberately NOT part of the approval hash — it changes every run, and a job that demanded approval daily would train you to approve without reading. So it reaches the model as notes ordered after the approved prompt, explicitly framed as observations that lose to the instructions.

closer.title: Where it lives
closer.body: The Automations page in the sidebar, or dreamcontext automations create <slug> --title "…" --days daily --at 18:00. Live-test it with automations run <slug> --force before you trust it to the schedule.
